questions.question: What is the primary role of the IP layer in the Internet protocol stack?
options: Detect and correct transmission errors at the link level
Determine the next hop for each packet toward its destination
Ensure reliable end-to-end delivery of application data
Establish virtual circuits for session management
Translate domain names into IP addresses
questions.explanation:
IP provides destination-based, best-effort delivery across different networks. A router uses the destination IP address and its forwarding table to select the next hop for each datagram. This does not promise reliable or ordered delivery: recovery belongs to TCP or the application. Link error handling and DNS name resolution serve different layers and do not replace IP forwarding.

See [IP and Internet architecture](../lessons/01_routing/01_internet_architecture.md).

questions.question: Which IP header field is primarily responsible for limiting the lifetime of a datagram in the network?
options: Total Length
Fragment Offset
Identification
Header Checksum
Time to Live
questions.explanation:
Time to Live (TTL) is reduced as an IPv4 datagram passes through routers. When it expires, the datagram is discarded, preventing a packet from circulating indefinitely in a forwarding loop. Total Length measures packet size, Fragment Offset identifies a fragment's position, and the checksum detects header corruption; none of those fields bounds the number of forwarding steps.

See [Reading an IPv4 header](../lessons/01_routing/02_ipv4_header.md).

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the behavior of ARP when a destination IP address is not found in the cache?
options: The router queries DNS for the MAC address
The packet is discarded and an ICMP error is returned
The node sends a broadcast to resolve the IP-to-MAC mapping
The packet is queued until the destination initiates contact
The node falls back to default gateway routing
questions.explanation:
An ARP cache miss triggers a broadcast request on the local Ethernet for the MAC address associated with the next-hop IPv4 address. The target replies and the sender caches the mapping. For an on-link destination the target is the destination itself; for a remote destination it is normally a gateway. DNS resolves names, not these local IP-to-MAC mappings.

See [IPv4 addresses, prefixes, and ARP](../lessons/01_routing/04_addressing_and_arp.md).

questions.question: Which of the following is a key limitation of the virtual circuit switching model compared to datagram switching?
options: It cannot guarantee in-order delivery
Packets can arrive out of sequence due to routing changes
It lacks mechanisms for resource reservation
Each packet must include the full destination address
It requires a connection setup phase before data transfer
questions.explanation:
A virtual-circuit network must first establish a logical path and install per-circuit state in intermediate switches. Data can then use the circuit identifier, but this setup adds delay and state-management work before transmission. Datagram switching can send each packet immediately using its destination address and existing routing state; it requires no corresponding per-connection path setup.

See [Routing, forwarding, and switching models](../lessons/01_routing/07_forwarding_and_switching.md).

questions.question: Which switching fabric architecture offers the highest aggregate throughput potential but becomes costly with increased port counts?
options: Self-routing switch
Shared memory switch
Crossbar switch
Token ring switch
Shared bus switch

questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the benefit of Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR)?
options: It increases header size to accommodate additional subnet information
It guarantees unique global IP addresses through manual allocation
It requires all IP addresses to belong to Class A, B, or C
It eliminates the need for ARP in local networks
It enables finer-grained route aggregation using variable-length prefixes
questions.explanation:
CIDR replaces the fixed class A/B/C boundaries with explicitly stated prefix lengths. An operator can allocate blocks closer to actual network needs and aggregate contiguous, properly aligned blocks under a shorter shared prefix. That can reduce the number of globally advertised routes. CIDR changes address allocation and route representation; it does not eliminate ARP or enlarge the IPv4 address field.

See [CIDR, aggregation, and longest-prefix matching](../lessons/01_routing/08_cidr_and_aggregation.md).

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of split horizon with poison reverse in distance vector routing?
options: Prevent routing loops caused by inconsistent neighbor state
Increase convergence speed during route advertisement
Guarantee shortest-path delivery through centralized updates
Compress routing tables for storage efficiency
Detect incorrect checksum values in packet headers
questions.explanation:
If B reaches a destination through C, poison reverse tells C that B's distance to that destination is infinite. C should therefore not mistake B for an independent working path back to it. This reduces simple two-router loops caused by stale distance-vector information. It is a loop-mitigation technique, not centralized shortest-path computation or a guarantee against every longer routing loop.

See [Routing loops and poison reverse](../lessons/01_routing/12_routing_loops.md).

questions.question: Which statement best characterizes the difference between link-state and distance-vector routing?
options: Link-state protocols require each node to flood full routing tables periodically
Link-state builds a global view of the network; distance-vector relies on local updates
Distance-vector is more scalable but requires more global knowledge
Distance-vector uses Dijkstra's algorithm; link-state uses Bellman-Ford
Link-state protocols exchange only next-hop costs; distance-vector sends topology maps
questions.explanation:
Link-state routers disseminate local link descriptions so each can construct a topology map and compute its own shortest paths. Distance-vector routers instead exchange destination-cost estimates with direct neighbors and combine those estimates with local link costs. Thus the distinction is global topology knowledge versus neighbor-based estimates, not whether route computation happens locally: it happens locally in both approaches.

See [Distance-vector routing and Bellman–Ford](../lessons/01_routing/11_distance_vector.md); [Link-state routing and shortest paths](../lessons/01_routing/10_link_state.md).

questions.question: In Dijkstra’s algorithm, what determines the next node to be added to the set of incorporated nodes?
options: The node with the largest number of incoming edges
The node with the longest sequence number in LSPs
The node with the fewest neighbors not yet visited
The node with the lowest total cost from the source
The node with the smallest hop count from any source
questions.explanation:
Dijkstra selects the unconfirmed node with the smallest tentative total distance from the source, confirms that distance, and relaxes the node's outgoing edges. It does not select merely the cheapest last link or the node with the fewest neighbors. With tentative distances B=2 and C=5, B is selected first; a later path through B may then improve C's distance.

See [Link-state routing and shortest paths](../lessons/01_routing/10_link_state.md).

questions.question: Why is longest prefix match essential in IP forwarding under CIDR?
options: It minimizes routing table lookup latency by reducing match entries
It reduces packet fragmentation during routing
It ensures packets are always sent to the physically nearest router
It guarantees load balancing across all equal-cost paths
It selects the route with the most specific network match to a destination IP
questions.explanation:
Several CIDR entries can match one destination because an aggregate and a more-specific exception may coexist. Longest-prefix matching chooses the entry fixing the largest number of destination bits. For example, 192.0.2.130 matches both 192.0.2.0/24 and 192.0.2.128/25, so the /25 wins. This is specificity, not a guarantee of nearest geography or equal-cost load balancing.

See [CIDR, aggregation, and longest-prefix matching](../lessons/01_routing/08_cidr_and_aggregation.md).

questions.question: Which of the following is a key tradeoff when choosing trie-based forwarding tables over TCAMs?
options: TCAMs support only exact-match queries, limiting CIDR use
TCAMs provide faster updates but lower lookup speed
Tries require specialized hardware, unlike TCAMs
Tries are software-friendly but slower for longest prefix match
Tries consume more power but offer constant-time lookups

questions.question: How does the choice of switching technique affect end-to-end delay in high-speed routers?
options: Crossbar switches reduce contention, lowering delay under load
Output queuing leads to minimal queuing delay regardless of load
Input queuing eliminates head-of-line blocking entirely
Shared-memory switches guarantee constant end-to-end delay
Virtual circuits always outperform datagram switching for delay

questions.question: Which of the following is a tradeoff introduced by Network Address Translation (NAT) in IPv4 networks?
options: NAT enables reuse of private address space but complicates inbound connections
NAT guarantees end-to-end packet integrity and IP transparency
NAT allows direct access to devices behind firewalls without port forwarding
NAT increases IPv6 adoption by embedding IPsec in every datagram
NAT simplifies peer-to-peer applications by removing stateful mappings

questions.question: Why is Network Address Translation (NAT) said to violate the end-to-end principle?
options: It changes destination MAC addresses during each hop
It prioritizes routing metrics over application-layer behavior
It obscures host identity by altering source IP and port fields
It tunnels datagrams using overlay protocols without notice
It blocks packets that use TCP options for performance
questions.explanation:
The end-to-end principle places functions needing endpoint knowledge at the network edges. NAT inserts an intermediary that rewrites network addresses and often transport ports, so the identifiers observed outside the translated network differ from the internal endpoint identifiers. This weakens address transparency and makes communication depend on an intermediary translation. Ordinary per-link MAC changes are a different mechanism.

See [Why IPv6 exists](../lessons/03_ipv6/01_motivation.md); [IP and Internet architecture](../lessons/01_routing/01_internet_architecture.md).

questions.question: Why is fast convergence especially critical in intra-domain (intra-AS) routing protocols?
options: Because intra-AS networks use satellite links with high delays
Because external ASes rely on interior routers to forward their packets
Because intra-AS routing updates are encrypted and hard to verify
Because routing loops can persist longer due to fixed BGP timers
Because failures inside the AS must be handled without notifying BGP
questions.explanation:
**Review note:** Fast intra-AS convergence restores usable internal forwarding and BGP next-hop reachability after a failure. However, the preserved key's claim that failures must be handled without notifying BGP is too absolute: an internal failure can make an external next hop unreachable and require BGP changes. Local recovery can contain some failures, but it does not guarantee that every failure remains invisible to inter-domain routing.

See [Convergence, failures, and stability](../lessons/01_routing/22_convergence.md); [Autonomous systems and routing domains](../lessons/01_routing/09_autonomous_systems.md); [BGP messages, routing state, and next hops](../lessons/01_routing/16_bgp_messages_and_state.md).

questions.question: How does the count-to-infinity problem arise in distance vector routing?
options: Routers misconfigure metric weights and overestimate costs
Routers exchange full topology graphs without synchronization
Routing loops cause route advertisements to grow in cost indefinitely
TTL fields expire prematurely, causing route drops
Link-layer retransmissions interfere with routing updates
questions.explanation:
After a failure, neighboring routers can each advertise a stale route that actually depends on the other. Each then adds its link cost to the neighbor's claimed distance, increasing the advertised metric while retaining a loop. Counting ends at the protocol's chosen infinity value; it is not necessarily numerically unbounded. TTL limits individual packets but does not correct the stale routing estimates.

See [Routing loops and poison reverse](../lessons/01_routing/12_routing_loops.md); [Distance-vector routing and Bellman–Ford](../lessons/01_routing/11_distance_vector.md).

questions.question: Under what network conditions does link-state routing outperform distance-vector routing?
options: When topologies are static and routing loops are tolerable
When link failures occur frequently and convergence time matters
When end-to-end delays are symmetric and predictable
When routers are added slowly and metrics remain constant
When routing decisions depend solely on local neighbor costs
questions.explanation:
**Review note:** Frequent failures make convergence behavior important, and link-state flooding followed by local shortest-path computation can avoid the stale-neighbor estimates behind distance-vector count-to-infinity. That motivates the keyed choice. It is not a universal performance ranking: topology, update propagation, timers, and implementation affect recovery, so frequent failures alone do not prove that every link-state protocol outperforms every distance-vector protocol.

See [Link-state routing and shortest paths](../lessons/01_routing/10_link_state.md); [Distance-vector routing and Bellman–Ford](../lessons/01_routing/11_distance_vector.md); [Routing loops and poison reverse](../lessons/01_routing/12_routing_loops.md).

questions.question: How does OSPF ensure all routers in an area compute consistent shortest paths?
options: By flooding link-state advertisements and running Dijkstra locally
By relying on round-robin updates via a designated gateway
By using BGP path attributes to prioritize paths
By synchronizing timers across all routers
By distributing a global topology map through distance vectors
questions.explanation:
**Supplementary (†):** This answer uses teaching marked supplementary in the supplied guide.

OSPF reliably floods LSAs within their appropriate scope, allowing routers in an area to synchronize their link-state databases. Each router then runs Dijkstra locally on that topology to calculate routes from its own position. They share topology information, not identical forwarding tables or a central route computation; their next hops naturally depend on where each router sits.

See [OSPF areas and protocol operation](../lessons/01_routing/14_ospf.md); [Link-state routing and shortest paths](../lessons/01_routing/10_link_state.md).

questions.question: What is the primary scalability benefit of organizing OSPF into areas?
options: It limits LSA flooding scope, reducing control message overhead
It permits routers to select different link-layer protocols
It shifts routing decisions to centralized OSPF root servers
It allows routers to ignore global addressing formats
It enables routing based solely on MAC address learning
questions.explanation:
**Supplementary (†):** This answer uses teaching marked supplementary in the supplied guide.

OSPF areas confine detailed topology information and much LSA flooding to manageable scopes. Routers retain their own area's detail while using inter-area reachability through area border routers for other areas. This reduces the topology and update burden compared with requiring every router to maintain every link in a large AS. It does not introduce centralized OSPF root servers.

See [OSPF areas and protocol operation](../lessons/01_routing/14_ospf.md).

questions.question: Why does inter-domain routing prioritize policy over optimality?
options: Because distance-vector algorithms always produce routing loops at scale
Because IP addresses change dynamically within each AS
Because it must ensure MAC-level broadcast domains remain isolated
Because shortest-path routing often conflicts with administrative preferences
Because link-state protocols cannot scale to the size of the global Internet
questions.explanation:
Each AS has its own commercial, operational, and security preferences. A route with fewer hops can be unacceptable if it would provide unpaid transit or violate an export policy. BGP therefore selects permitted, preferred reachability rather than one universally shortest path across the Internet. Scale matters too, but independent administrative policy is the essential reason shortest-path optimality is not the sole goal.

See [Why BGP uses paths and policy](../lessons/01_routing/15_bgp_path_vector.md); [Business relationships and export policy](../lessons/01_routing/18_bgp_export_policy.md).

questions.question: How does BGP use path vector routing to prevent persistent loops?
options: By incrementing a loop counter in each UPDATE message
By requiring routers to flood link-state advertisements
By discarding all routes containing multiple equal-cost paths
By tagging each route with the sequence of ASes traversed
By ignoring prefix advertisements from transit providers
questions.explanation:
BGP advertises the sequence of ASes associated with a route in AS_PATH. A receiving speaker normally rejects a route containing its own ASN, because accepting it would advertise an AS-level path back through itself. External propagation normally adds the advertising AS's ASN. This prevents advertised AS-path loops; it does not replace packet TTL or eliminate every transient forwarding inconsistency.

See [Why BGP uses paths and policy](../lessons/01_routing/15_bgp_path_vector.md).

questions.question: What role does the BGP UPDATE message play in maintaining Internet-wide routing?
options: It synchronizes router clocks to ensure global loop prevention
It provides guaranteed packet delivery through ACKs and retransmissions
It encodes AS policies using OSPF-compatible link-state data
It installs new routes and withdraws obsolete ones between BGP peers
It broadcasts Ethernet-level neighbor discovery information
questions.explanation:
An UPDATE announces reachable prefixes with path attributes or withdraws reachability previously advertised to a peer. The receiver evaluates these changes under its own policy and next-hop reachability before choosing routes. UPDATE therefore maintains distributed control-plane routing information; it does not itself guarantee packet delivery or force every receiver to install the advertised route.

See [BGP messages, routing state, and next hops](../lessons/01_routing/16_bgp_messages_and_state.md).

questions.question: How do the LOCAL_PREF and AS_PATH attributes influence BGP route selection?
options: LOCAL_PREF favors longer AS paths to improve resilience
AS_PATH is used only to detect packet loss at the link layer
LOCAL_PREF encodes IP precedence values from application headers
AS_PATH ensures that updates are rate-limited by time intervals
LOCAL_PREF applies within a single AS to prefer specific exits
questions.explanation:
**Review note:** Higher LOCAL_PREF expresses a preferred route or exit within an AS. For otherwise comparable candidates, shorter AS_PATH can be preferred later in the selection process, so stronger local policy can outweigh a shorter path. The preserved keyed option describes LOCAL_PREF but leaves out AS_PATH and their ordering; it is incomplete as an answer to the full stem.

See [BGP route selection and internal sessions](../lessons/01_routing/17_bgp_route_selection.md).

questions.question: How can an autonomous system (AS) prevent certain prefixes from being advertised to specific neighbors?
options: By applying prefix filters in BGP export policies
By using OSPF area boundaries to mask internal prefixes
By increasing the LOCAL_PREF value beyond maximum range
By configuring the TTL field to expire near border routers
By setting IP fragmentation flags to restrict propagation
questions.explanation:
An export prefix filter permits or denies particular destination prefixes in advertisements to a selected BGP neighbor. Applying a suitable filter can therefore prevent that neighbor from learning prefixes the AS does not intend to export. LOCAL_PREF influences local route selection, while TTL and fragmentation flags affect data packets; those mechanisms do not directly implement per-neighbor advertisement filtering.

See [Business relationships and export policy](../lessons/01_routing/18_bgp_export_policy.md).

questions.question: Why do ASes in a peer-to-peer relationship typically avoid acting as transit for each other's traffic?
options: Because peers are required to route traffic via a central registrar
Because peer-to-peer links use lower-cost copper cables
Because BGP lacks support for policy-based filtering between peers
Because peers must run identical link-state protocols internally
Because carrying third-party traffic offers no economic benefit
questions.explanation:
**Review note:** Peers do exchange agreed traffic, typically between their own networks and customer cones. The economic restriction concerns providing unpaid transit from one peer or provider to another unrelated network. Under the usual policy, peer-learned routes are exported to customers but not to other peers or providers. The keyed economic rationale should not be read as saying peers never carry traffic for each other.

See [Business relationships and export policy](../lessons/01_routing/18_bgp_export_policy.md).

questions.question: What routing anomaly can occur if an AS violates the valley-free routing principle?
options: It disables BGP UPDATE messages on internal interfaces
It can reduce the TTL of all received packets to zero
It may unintentionally advertise transit routes for peers and providers
It causes iBGP routers to announce the same route multiple times
It leads to inconsistent MAC address resolution at border routers
questions.explanation:
Under typical valley-free policies, routes learned from a peer or provider are exported only to customers. Exporting such a route to another peer or provider can attract traffic that makes the AS an unintended transit network. That is a route leak or policy violation; it does not require a malformed packet header or failure of BGP's UPDATE mechanism.

See [Business relationships and export policy](../lessons/01_routing/18_bgp_export_policy.md); [BGP hijacks and route leaks](../lessons/01_routing/19_bgp_hijacks_and_leaks.md).

questions.question: How do export filters help reinforce economic relationships in BGP routing?
options: By controlling which routes are advertised to peers and providers
By rejecting all routes with AS_PATH lengths exceeding a threshold
By rerouting traffic toward slower but cheaper backup paths
By modifying IP headers to prioritize paying traffic
By adjusting path MTU values based on AS type
questions.explanation:
Export filters control which prefixes each neighbor is told the AS can reach. Combined with customer, provider, and peer relationships, they prevent advertisements that would attract unpaid or unauthorized transit traffic. They enforce economic policy in the control plane; they do not need to rewrite data-packet headers or adjust MTU values.

See [Business relationships and export policy](../lessons/01_routing/18_bgp_export_policy.md).

questions.question: What causes path exploration to slow down BGP convergence after a link failure?
options: The routing table must be rebuilt from scratch by all ASes
BGP routers broadcast ARP requests during link changes
Multiple invalid alternate paths are briefly accepted and then withdrawn
The TTL of all prefixes must be extended during failure events
AS_PATH values are encrypted and delay route processing

questions.question: Why does iBGP require a full mesh or route reflectors to function correctly?
options: Because iBGP lacks UPDATE messages and relies on TCP flooding
Because iBGP routers cannot determine MAC addresses of peers
Because iBGP performs NAT at each AS border by default
Because iBGP does not propagate routes learned from other iBGP peers
Because iBGP must recompute shortest paths using OSPF weights

questions.question: What is a tradeoff introduced by using route reflectors in iBGP to reduce full mesh requirements?
options: Route reflectors must be external to the AS and use eBGP instead
Route reflectors require per-neighbor OSPF flooding
Route reflectors disable TCP-based message authentication
Route reflectors violate the valley-free routing model
Route reflectors can introduce path asymmetries or suboptimal routes

questions.question: Why is BGP particularly vulnerable to prefix hijacking attacks?
options: It requires ASes to re-announce their prefixes hourly
It only supports hop-by-hop MAC address validation
It lacks global authentication of advertised prefixes
It uses fixed-length subnet masks for all advertisements
It encrypts routing updates, delaying propagation
questions.explanation:
Basic BGP accepts a neighbor's reachability claims without cryptographic proof that the announcing AS is authorized to originate each prefix. An unauthorized announcement can therefore attract traffic, especially if it is more specific than a legitimate aggregate and wins longest-prefix matching. This is why normal routing operation can propagate a hijack even when packet forwarding follows its configured rules.

See [BGP hijacks and route leaks](../lessons/01_routing/19_bgp_hijacks_and_leaks.md).

questions.question: How does RPKI improve BGP security compared to the traditional model?
options: By encrypting all BGP routing updates with symmetric keys
By rewriting IP headers at IXPs to match verified policies
By limiting the number of peering sessions per AS
By authenticating AS_PATHs using DHCP-assigned policies
By verifying route origin using cryptographically signed prefix-authority mappings
questions.explanation:
RPKI provides signed authorizations connecting address resources, permitted origin ASNs, and allowed prefix lengths. Route origin validation can compare a BGP announcement with those authorizations and classify the claimed origin. Operators must still apply a policy to the result. This improves origin checking; it neither encrypts UPDATE messages nor authenticates every AS_PATH hop.

See [RPKI and route origin validation](../lessons/01_routing/20_rpki.md).

questions.question: Which of the following best illustrates the separation between control and data planes in modern networks?
options: Load balancers directing traffic based on TLS certificate content
NAT rewriting headers during TCP connection establishment
DNS resolving hostnames to IP addresses using recursive queries
ARP resolving MAC addresses across autonomous systems
Routers forwarding packets based on a table computed by a distinct routing protocol
questions.explanation:
Routing protocols and policy compute the control-plane state from which a forwarding table is installed. The data plane then uses that table to send individual packets to their next hops. This separates calculating forwarding behavior from executing it. DNS name resolution, ARP neighbor resolution, and NAT rewriting do not by themselves illustrate that routing-versus-forwarding division.

See [Routing, forwarding, and switching models](../lessons/01_routing/07_forwarding_and_switching.md).

questions.question: What kind of network behavior can traceroute help identify that routing tables alone might miss?
options: Fragmentation anomalies at the application layer
Incorrect NAT bindings on UDP-based firewalls
DNS spoofing events inside a local subnet
BGP loop prevention settings at the IXPs
Forwarding inconsistencies caused by policy-based routing or failures
questions.explanation:
A routing table describes a device's installed next-hop choices, while traceroute gathers evidence from probes sent along the forwarding path. Comparing the two can reveal unexpected hops or behavior following policy changes and failures. Traceroute does not uniquely diagnose the cause: missing ICMP replies can reflect filtering or rate limiting even while packets continue to be forwarded.

See [ICMP, ping, and traceroute](../lessons/01_routing/05_icmp_and_diagnostics.md).

questions.question: What is a potential limitation of using Equal-Cost Multi-Path (ECMP) routing based on flow hashing?
options: It always results in packet reordering across all flows
It prevents path failure detection due to static routing tables
It disables MPLS label switching at edge routers
It can lead to uneven load distribution when many flows hash to the same path
It requires each flow to be acknowledged by all available paths

questions.question: Why is IP anycast particularly suitable for services like DNS root servers?
options: It avoids BGP convergence delays by using static host routes
It ensures all queries are answered by the same replica for consistency
It establishes persistent TCP sessions across all replicas simultaneously
It directs clients to a nearby instance without requiring client-side changes
It guarantees full application-layer failover using HTTP redirects
questions.explanation:
Anycast lets multiple DNS sites advertise the same service address or prefix. A resolver sends an ordinary query to that address, and routing selects a preferred reachable instance without requiring the client to choose a site-specific destination. Nearby means favorable according to routing policy and metrics, not guaranteed physical proximity. Failure recovery still depends on detection, route withdrawal, convergence, and retries.

See [Anycast DNS and routing-based recovery](../lessons/02_dns/18_anycast_and_resilience.md).

questions.question: What is a challenge introduced by using IP anycast for DNS service deployment?
options: Anycast disables local caching of DNS records
Anycast routes only to IPv6 endpoints, not IPv4
Anycast prevents TCP queries from reaching authoritative servers
Clients may receive inconsistent responses if routed to different replicas
DNSSEC cannot be used over anycast due to key distribution limits
questions.explanation:
Anycast can send clients using one service address to different replicas. If those replicas are at different points in a zone update, they can temporarily return different data; resolver caches can also retain older answers until TTL expiry. The risk comes from replica and cache timing, not an inherent inability of anycast to serve consistent data. Combine replication timing with routing-based instance selection.

See [Replication, SOA, and cache lifetimes](../lessons/02_dns/08_replication_and_caching.md); [Anycast DNS and routing-based recovery](../lessons/02_dns/18_anycast_and_resilience.md).

questions.question: Which BGP mechanism allows a multihomed AS to influence incoming traffic from different providers?
options: Broadcasting MAC addresses across upstream ASes
Injecting traceroute paths into the routing table
Adjusting the OSPF cost for internal links
Prepending its own AS multiple times in route advertisements
Disabling BGP UPDATE messages for backup providers
questions.explanation:
AS-path prepending repeats the advertising AS's own ASN, making one advertised path appear longer. An AS can apply it selectively on provider-facing advertisements to discourage incoming traffic through that provider. Remote networks still apply their own policies, so a stronger preference such as LOCAL_PREF can outweigh the extra path length. This influences inbound choice rather than directly programming another AS's forwarding table.

See [Convergence, failures, and stability](../lessons/01_routing/22_convergence.md); [BGP route selection and internal sessions](../lessons/01_routing/17_bgp_route_selection.md).

questions.question: Why is convergence typically slower in inter-domain routing compared to intra-domain routing?
options: Because intra-domain routing lacks support for failure recovery
Because inter-domain updates depend on physical cable types
Because inter-domain routing uses shorter prefix lengths
Because inter-domain policies delay or filter route propagation
Because intra-domain routers must wait for eBGP to stabilize first
questions.explanation:
Inter-domain routes pass through independently operated ASes that rank and filter advertisements according to different policies. A change can trigger a sequence of withdrawals and alternative selections, and some policy combinations can oscillate. An IGP operates within one administrative domain and a more coordinated metric model. This explains why BGP convergence can be slower; it is not a fixed timing guarantee for every network.

See [Convergence, failures, and stability](../lessons/01_routing/22_convergence.md); [Why BGP uses paths and policy](../lessons/01_routing/15_bgp_path_vector.md); [Business relationships and export policy](../lessons/01_routing/18_bgp_export_policy.md).

questions.question: Which of the following best illustrates the functional separation between routing and forwarding?
options: Forwarding updates route metrics based on congestion state
Forwarding protocols advertise AS_PATHs to external peers
Routing determines packet checksums at each hop
Forwarding executes per-packet lookups based on routing-derived tables
Routing applies encryption to payloads before transit
questions.explanation:
Routing learns or computes reachability and selects the rules installed for forwarding. Forwarding applies those rules to each arriving packet, typically through a destination-prefix lookup in the FIB. A router need not rerun its routing algorithm for every packet. Updating route metrics and advertising paths are control-plane work rather than the per-packet lookup itself.

See [Routing, forwarding, and switching models](../lessons/01_routing/07_forwarding_and_switching.md).

questions.question: Why is hierarchical routing essential for large-scale network scalability?
options: It hides link failures by tunneling control messages
It prevents routing loops using Time-to-Live (TTL) mechanisms
It disables inter-AS forwarding unless pre-approved by IANA
It increases the bit-length of subnet masks in local routers
It limits the scope of routing updates to manageable areas
questions.explanation:
**Supplementary (†):** This answer uses teaching marked supplementary in the supplied guide.

Routing hierarchy reduces how much detail every router must track and how widely every update must propagate. In OSPF, routers retain local area topology while ABRs provide inter-area reachability through the backbone. That keeps flooding and state within more manageable scopes. Hierarchy does not work by enlarging address fields or hiding every failure through tunnels.

See [OSPF areas and protocol operation](../lessons/01_routing/14_ospf.md); [CIDR, aggregation, and longest-prefix matching](../lessons/01_routing/08_cidr_and_aggregation.md).

questions.question: Which key distinction separates distance-vector from link-state routing algorithms?
options: Link-state algorithms build a global view before computing routes
Distance-vector ignores next-hop cost when updating metrics
Link-state routes are computed by neighbors and pushed downstream
Distance-vector requires flooding of topology updates to all routers
Distance-vector uses full network maps to calculate shortest paths
questions.explanation:
Link-state routers first obtain a topology description through flooding and then independently compute routes, commonly using Dijkstra. Distance-vector routers use neighboring cost estimates and add their own link costs through Bellman–Ford. The key difference is the information available to each router; distance-vector does not require each router to receive a complete topology map.

See [Distance-vector routing and Bellman–Ford](../lessons/01_routing/11_distance_vector.md); [Link-state routing and shortest paths](../lessons/01_routing/10_link_state.md).

questions.question: What makes BGP both powerful and risky in inter-domain routing?
options: It automatically encrypts all route updates and hides AS identity
It forces routers to recompute shortest paths after every packet
It enables flexible policy enforcement but lacks route authenticity checks
It supports path vector routing but requires centralized control
It enforces consistent metrics across all ASes without exception
questions.explanation:
BGP lets operators independently rank and export routes, which gives it the flexibility needed for commercial and administrative policy. Basic route advertisements do not, by themselves, prove prefix authorization or proper export behavior, so a mistaken or malicious claim can spread. Security mechanisms and filters add checks, but policy flexibility alone does not provide authenticity.

See [BGP hijacks and route leaks](../lessons/01_routing/19_bgp_hijacks_and_leaks.md); [Why BGP uses paths and policy](../lessons/01_routing/15_bgp_path_vector.md); [Business relationships and export policy](../lessons/01_routing/18_bgp_export_policy.md).

questions.question: What is a common risk associated with overly permissive BGP export policies?
options: They cause routers to ignore default routes and drop all traffic
They force neighboring ASes to run OSPF instead of BGP
They disable shortest path computation inside the exporting AS
They increase the maximum length of AS_PATH attributes
They may unintentionally allow an AS to become a transit for unwanted prefixes
questions.explanation:
Advertising a route invites neighbors to send traffic toward the advertising AS. If its export policy permits routes learned from one peer or provider to reach another peer or provider, the AS can unintentionally offer transit it never agreed to supply. Relationship-aware export filtering restricts that propagation; overly permissive filters can therefore create reachability that is economically or operationally unwanted.

See [Business relationships and export policy](../lessons/01_routing/18_bgp_export_policy.md).

questions.question: Why is observability of the control plane behavior a key challenge in inter-domain routing?
options: Because control messages are broadcast over link-layer multicast
Because routing loops cannot be detected by traceroute
Because BGP hides the internal topology of neighboring ASes
Because BGP routers use randomized TTLs to confuse observers
Because data plane forwarding is always encrypted end-to-end
questions.explanation:
A BGP advertisement describes prefix reachability and an AS-level path rather than the complete router-and-link topology inside each neighboring AS. External observers therefore cannot reconstruct every internal decision from the advertisement alone. Additional policy choices may also remain private. This limits control-plane observability without requiring encrypted routing tables or randomized data-packet TTLs.

See [Why BGP uses paths and policy](../lessons/01_routing/15_bgp_path_vector.md).

questions.question: What makes the Internet particularly difficult to debug from a routing perspective?
options: Control-plane decisions are often hidden and influenced by opaque policies
Applications use symmetric NAT to bypass standard routing
All routing tables are encrypted and hosted on external DNS servers
Routers actively drop ICMP packets to preserve privacy
TCP headers are stripped before forwarding in core networks
questions.explanation:
End-to-end paths result from decisions made by independent ASes, each applying its own rankings and export restrictions. Other operators often cannot inspect those policies or internal topology, so a local symptom can depend on a hidden remote decision. The difficulty is decentralized, incomplete visibility; it is not that BGP tables must be encrypted or that TCP headers disappear at core routers.

See [Why BGP uses paths and policy](../lessons/01_routing/15_bgp_path_vector.md); [Business relationships and export policy](../lessons/01_routing/18_bgp_export_policy.md).

questions.question: How does TCP handle sequence number wraparound after long connections?
options: It resets the connection and reestablishes new initial sequence numbers
It uses modulo arithmetic to compare and interpret sequence numbers
It re-encodes segment headers using 64-bit values instead of 32-bit
It ignores all acknowledgments until the next window opens
It flushes out-of-order segments and closes the connection

questions.question: Under what conditions does TCP unnecessarily retransmit data, and how can this be mitigated?
options: When acknowledgments are reordered, triggering spurious fast retransmits
When data is sent via UDP and received on TCP
When packets are dropped due to ECN markings in IPv6 headers
When the advertised window is zero and retransmit timer is too short
When TCP options are misconfigured to use SACK only

questions.question: What are the consequences of accepting only in-order TCP segments, and how does it differ from standard TCP behavior?
options: It enables rapid congestion avoidance but increases round-trip delay
It blocks out-of-order data that standard TCP would buffer for reassembly
It simplifies sender logic but reduces reliability for long-lived connections
It prevents window updates from being processed during loss episodes
It improves bandwidth by avoiding retransmissions of duplicate ACKs
questions.explanation:
A TCP receiver can retain segments that arrive beyond a missing byte range while continuing to deliver application data in order. When the gap is filled, a cumulative ACK can cover the newly contiguous data, including those buffered bytes. An implementation that discards all out-of-order segments instead wastes that progress and may require them to be retransmitted. Buffering out-of-order arrivals does not mean delivering them out of order.

See [Reno fast recovery and out-of-order buffering](../lessons/04_tcp/14_reno_fast_recovery.md).

questions.question: What could happen if the TTL field in the IP header is misconfigured or not decremented correctly?
options: It causes packet reordering across multipath routes
It prevents fragmentation by setting the DF flag
It disables IPsec authentication at the receiving host
It allows packets caught in loops to circulate indefinitely
It forces ARP table updates at each hop
questions.explanation:
**Review note:** A forwarding loop cannot retain an individual packet indefinitely when routers correctly decrement TTL and discard the packet at expiry. If that decrement behavior is broken, the TTL protection can fail, which is the interpretation supporting the preserved key. Merely choosing a large legal initial TTL only permits more hops; it is not equivalent to disabling the decrement mechanism.

See [Reading an IPv4 header](../lessons/01_routing/02_ipv4_header.md); [Routing loops and poison reverse](../lessons/01_routing/12_routing_loops.md).

questions.question: How can ECN help reduce packet loss in IP networks, and what is a key limitation?
options: ECN marks packets before drops but requires both endpoints to support it
ECN prevents congestion by switching to TCP Reno under load
ECN reduces loss by buffering traffic at the application layer
ECN disables TCP retransmissions during congestion
ECN adjusts TTL to avoid saturated routers
questions.explanation:
With ECN, a capable network device can mark congestion in an eligible packet instead of immediately relying on a drop as its signal. Capable endpoints must convey and react to that signal for congestion control to reduce load. This can avoid some losses, but does not eliminate congestion or all packet drops, and endpoint support alone does not ensure every network path performs ECN marking.

See [Reading an IPv4 header](../lessons/01_routing/02_ipv4_header.md).

questions.question: What role does the fragment offset field play in IP reassembly, and how can overlapping fragments be exploited?
options: It limits packet size based on hop count
It identifies the destination host’s MTU for upstream routing
It enables simultaneous transmission of TCP and UDP in a single datagram
It specifies whether packets should be routed via core routers
It determines where each fragment fits in the original packet, which can be manipulated to overwrite valid data

questions.question: Why might allowing all ICMP message types through a firewall pose security or stability risks?
options: ICMP messages can be used to reroute TCP packets via alternate ports
ICMP disables checksum verification when fragmented
Some ICMP types can reveal internal topology or facilitate DoS attacks
ICMP packets are converted into unicast ARP messages
Allowing ICMP breaks DNSSEC integrity validation

questions.question: How can ICMP Redirect messages introduce security or stability issues in a network?
options: They fragment IP packets to reduce performance
They increase ARP traffic by forcing host reconfiguration
They bypass firewalls by rewriting TCP headers
They allow malicious routers to influence host routing tables
They disable ECMP hashing in multi-path networks

questions.question: What happens when a NAT device using port overloading exhausts its available port space?
options: It switches to a static NAT mapping scheme for new flows
It increases the TTL to delay flow termination
It drops new outbound connections or reuses ports, risking collisions
It resets all active connections to free resources
It tunnels all subsequent packets through IPv6 encapsulation

questions.question: Which technique enables two peers behind NATs to establish direct connectivity, and what is a key limitation?
options: TCP Fast Open bypasses NATs using TLS probes
UPnP automates firewall configuration but requires manual keying
STUN allows peers to discover public IP/port but fails with symmetric NATs
DHCP relay solves NAT traversal by extending subnet masks
SNMP triggers NAT rebinding using flow tables

questions.question: What function do OSPF Area Border Routers (ABRs) serve in a hierarchical network?
options: They encrypt control traffic between backbone and stub areas
They aggregate LSAs to reduce update scope between areas
They act as DHCP relays in multi-area domains
They override OSPF metrics using administrative distance
They inject external BGP routes into all OSPF areas
questions.explanation:
**Supplementary (†):** This answer uses teaching marked supplementary in the supplied guide.

**Review note:** ABRs connect OSPF areas and provide summarized inter-area reachability so detailed topology need not flood everywhere. The keyed phrase aggregate LSAs is shorthand that can mislead: ABRs originate appropriate summary information rather than simply merging arbitrary received LSAs and forwarding them unchanged across areas. The relevant benefit is bounded topology scope and manageable inter-area routing.

See [OSPF areas and protocol operation](../lessons/01_routing/14_ospf.md); [Link-state routing and shortest paths](../lessons/01_routing/10_link_state.md).

questions.question: What can happen if the BGP NEXT_HOP attribute is misconfigured?
options: OSPF will override the BGP decision based on LSA types
Routers will drop packets due to TTL mismatches
BGP will merge paths from different ASes into a loop
The AS_PATH attribute will be incorrectly reset to null
Prefixes will be treated as unreachable due to invalid forwarding paths
questions.explanation:
A selected BGP route is useful for forwarding only if its NEXT_HOP can be resolved through suitable internal routing or a static route. A wrong or unreachable next-hop address can therefore make an advertised prefix unusable even when its AS_PATH looks acceptable. Receiving an UPDATE does not by itself establish a working packet-delivery path to that next hop.

See [BGP messages, routing state, and next hops](../lessons/01_routing/16_bgp_messages_and_state.md); [BGP route selection and internal sessions](../lessons/01_routing/17_bgp_route_selection.md).

questions.question: How do LOCAL_PREF and MED differ in BGP route selection, and what conflict can arise?
options: LOCAL_PREF applies only to eBGP, while MED applies only to OSPF
MED adjusts TTL for routes, whereas LOCAL_PREF affects ECMP balancing
MED always overrides LOCAL_PREF when received from external ASes
LOCAL_PREF is used within an AS, MED is used across AS boundaries
Conflicts arise because both override BGP’s loop detection rule
questions.explanation:
**Review note:** LOCAL_PREF expresses preference inside an AS, with higher values normally preferred. MED can be advertised by a neighbor to suggest a preferred entry point, usually comparing lower MED values from the same neighboring AS. The keyed option is an incomplete summary: MED is evaluated by the receiving AS, and a stronger LOCAL_PREF can override the neighbor's lower-MED preference. The stem's requested conflict is this policy disagreement.

See [BGP route selection and internal sessions](../lessons/01_routing/17_bgp_route_selection.md).

questions.question: What advantage does the BGP Community attribute provide, and what is one associated risk?
options: It adjusts TCP retransmission behavior under congestion
It enables compression of IP prefixes but requires OSPF support
It allows tagging of routes for shared policy enforcement, but can propagate unintended markings
It prevents MED conflicts by disabling local preferences
It replaces AS_PATH but increases loop formation probability

questions.question: How does the prefix length in CIDR notation impact both routing decisions and address allocation?
options: Longer prefixes mean larger subnet sizes and less efficient routing
Shorter prefixes increase aggregation but reduce routing precision
Prefix length only affects DNS lookups, not routing or allocation
Shorter prefixes result in more specific forwarding entries
Longer prefixes match more routes but reduce address utilization
questions.explanation:
A shorter prefix fixes fewer bits and covers a larger address range, making it suitable for an aggregate announcement. A longer prefix covers fewer addresses and allows a more-specific forwarding exception or smaller allocation. For example, /24 covers 256 address patterns while /25 covers 128. Aggregation therefore trades fewer advertised entries against less detail in that summary; longest-prefix matching still honors any installed specific exceptions.

See [CIDR, aggregation, and longest-prefix matching](../lessons/01_routing/08_cidr_and_aggregation.md); [IPv4 addresses, prefixes, and ARP](../lessons/01_routing/04_addressing_and_arp.md).

questions.question: What failure mode can occur from overly aggressive prefix aggregation in BGP?
options: Loss of reachability for disaggregated subnets (routing holes)
Increased convergence delay due to flooding of LSAs
Formation of microloops due to inconsistent ECMP hashing
Excessive NAT table usage across stub networks
Creation of infinite AS_PATHs from inconsistent MED values

questions.question: How can export prefix filtering help an AS defend against accidental route leaks?
options: It ensures that only authorized prefixes are advertised externally
It blocks BGP communities tagged as transit-only
It redirects traffic toward root DNS servers
It avoids TTL manipulation by upstream routers
It disables DNSSEC validation for untrusted domains
questions.explanation:
An export prefix filter checks an advertisement against the prefixes and relationships the AS intends to allow for that neighbor. Rejecting an unauthorized export can prevent a valid route from leaking beyond its permitted scope. A route leak is about propagation policy, so a legitimate origin alone is insufficient; the filter must reflect which routes may be sent to which peers or providers.

See [Business relationships and export policy](../lessons/01_routing/18_bgp_export_policy.md); [BGP hijacks and route leaks](../lessons/01_routing/19_bgp_hijacks_and_leaks.md).

questions.question: What limitation of classful IP addressing motivated the adoption of classless addressing (CIDR)?
options: Classful schemes had poor alignment with actual network size needs
Classful addressing used encrypted headers, hindering route lookup
Classful routing used OSPF instead of RIP, increasing complexity
CIDR reduced address reuse by enforcing fixed subnet sizes
CIDR increased MAC-to-IP mapping latency
questions.explanation:
Classful addressing forced networks into a few fixed block sizes, such as /8, /16, and /24. Those choices often fit actual needs poorly, wasting address space or requiring awkward allocation. CIDR specifies a variable prefix length so allocations can fit more closely and suitable blocks can be aggregated. This is an address-allocation and routing improvement, not a change to MAC resolution.

See [IPv4 addresses, prefixes, and ARP](../lessons/01_routing/04_addressing_and_arp.md).

questions.question: What is a key functional difference between the Forwarding Information Base (FIB) and the Routing Information Base (RIB)?
options: FIB handles ARP resolution; RIB manages TCP flow states
RIB applies BGP policies, while FIB buffers packets during link failure
FIB stores all protocol metrics, while RIB caches TTL values
RIB is queried per-packet, while FIB is updated by DNS servers
RIB holds the complete routing table; FIB is optimized for fast lookups
questions.explanation:
The RIB stores control-plane routing information used to choose routes. The FIB stores the installed forwarding actions in a form suited to fast per-packet lookups. Calling the RIB the complete routing table is a simplification: the important distinction is route knowledge and selection versus executable forwarding state. Neither database is a TCP flow-state table or a DNS-managed TTL cache.

See [Routing, forwarding, and switching models](../lessons/01_routing/07_forwarding_and_switching.md).

questions.question: What problem arises from head-of-line blocking in input-buffered routers?
options: It causes packets from one input to block others, reducing throughput
It creates infinite loops due to ARP resolution failures
It causes checksum collisions between packets from different sources
It increases TTL values beyond safe limits
It leads to exponential growth in routing table size

questions.question: Why does a shared bus architecture limit throughput in high-speed routers?
options: It enforces TTL synchronization across interfaces
Packets are serialized over a single data path, creating a bottleneck
IP headers must be compressed before transmission
Each packet must pass through both ingress and egress buffers
It duplicates packets for multicast by default

questions.question: What is a major challenge in using crossbar switch fabric in routers?
options: They require prefix compression for efficient route matching
The scheduler must resolve conflicts for simultaneous port requests
TCP congestion control must be embedded in the hardware
Crossbars cannot support full-duplex traffic
Crossbars introduce MTU fragmentation on long links

questions.question: How do multistage interconnection networks like Clos improve router scalability?
options: They route packets using VLAN tags to bypass loops
They eliminate the need for link-layer retransmissions
They parallelize switching using multiple internal paths
They reduce total port-to-port delay by eliminating buffering
They aggregate TCP segments across interfaces

questions.question: Why is TCAM commonly used for longest prefix match (LPM) in IP forwarding, and what is a key limitation?
options: TCAM supports flow hashing but requires link-state updates
TCAM buffers full routing tables and encrypts lookups
TCAM reduces BGP churn but increases MTU overhead
TCAM selects prefixes based on destination port availability
TCAM enables parallel prefix matching but is power-hungry and size-limited

questions.question: What causes persistent route oscillation in BGP and how can it be mitigated?
options: High TCP retransmission rates; switch to UDP-based peering
Loopback misconfiguration; solution is to enable ICMP redirects
TTL mismatch between routers; use of symmetric NATs
Conflicting LOCAL_PREF settings; coordination of policies needed
Inconsistent DSCP values; ECMP hash rebalancing required
questions.explanation:
Independent AS policies can prefer mutually incompatible routing outcomes, causing repeated selections and withdrawals rather than convergence. Conflicting local preferences are one way this can arise; reviewing and coordinating those policies addresses the underlying interaction. Merely speeding up updates or changing BGP's TCP transport does not make incompatible preferences consistent. Oscillation is different from a wedgie, which can be stable but unwanted.

See [Convergence, failures, and stability](../lessons/01_routing/22_convergence.md); [BGP route selection and internal sessions](../lessons/01_routing/17_bgp_route_selection.md); [BGP wedgies: stable but unwanted routes](../lessons/01_routing/23_bgp_wedgies.md).

questions.question: How does the AS-level customer-provider topology influence route propagation?
options: Providers always prefer peer routes to customer routes
Customers propagate all received routes upstream to ISPs
Route export policies restrict advertisement of peer routes to other peers
Stub ASes never advertise prefixes via BGP
Provider ASes use TTL=1 to prevent transit from downstream ASes
questions.explanation:
Under the usual customer-provider export pattern, an AS can advertise customer routes broadly because carrying that traffic serves paying customers. A route learned from a peer is normally exported only to customers, not to another peer or provider. These relationship-dependent restrictions shape which AS-level paths become visible; they are configured policy rather than an automatic BGP protocol guarantee.

See [Business relationships and export policy](../lessons/01_routing/18_bgp_export_policy.md).

questions.question: What is a likely consequence of a peering dispute between large ISPs?
options: The losing ISP is forced to adopt OSPF internally
Multicast routing replaces BGP across the peering link
End-to-end connectivity is disrupted between customers of each ISP
Peering disputes are handled by ICANN arbitration automatically
One ISP hijacks the other's prefixes using AS_PATH poisoning
questions.explanation:
A peering dispute can cause two networks to stop exchanging routes or carrying traffic under their previous agreement. Customers on opposite sides can then lose reachability when no permitted alternative path exists. The lecture's Level 3–Cogent example illustrates that commercial policy can disrupt connectivity despite functioning physical links. Neither automatic arbitration nor a change to OSPF or multicast is required.

See [Business relationships and export policy](../lessons/01_routing/18_bgp_export_policy.md).

questions.question: What is the tradeoff involved in applying route flap damping in BGP?
options: It disables route reflection in large ASes
It increases TCP retransmissions due to loss of reachability
It prevents load balancing by removing ECMP support
It forces route aggregation, reducing address space efficiency
It reduces control-plane traffic but may suppress legitimate route changes

questions.question: How does OSPF support fast reroute when a primary link fails?
options: By computing disjoint loop-free alternate paths in advance
By resetting TCP connections over affected paths
By switching to BGP until the OSPF database converges
By sending ICMP redirects to all neighbors immediately
By adjusting hop counts using DSCP fields

questions.question: Why does iBGP require a full mesh of sessions in a simple deployment?
options: To allow ECN marking across TCP connections
To propagate eBGP-learned routes across the AS without re-advertisement issues
To prevent loopback interface renumbering during failover
To ensure every router can send OSPF LSAs to external peers
To maintain shortest-path forwarding across Ethernet links

questions.question: How can differences in successive traceroute outputs suggest path instability?
options: Duplicate echo replies confirm NAT table overflow
Changing TTLs indicate hosts have restarted
The absence of SYN-ACKs shows TCP congestion
Repeated ICMP unreachable errors mean DNS spoofing is active
Fluctuating intermediate hops imply load balancing or route flapping

questions.question: Why is it recommended to establish iBGP sessions using loopback addresses?
options: Loopbacks are stable identifiers unaffected by physical interface failures
Loopbacks allow route aggregation at the IP layer
Loopbacks allow automatic configuration of BGP MED values
Loopbacks enable ECMP to distribute BGP updates
Loopbacks avoid path MTU discovery issues on BGP traffic

questions.question: How does the hierarchical ISP structure shape interdomain route propagation?
options: Stub ASes are required to act as route reflectors
Only Tier-2 ISPs are allowed to filter routes
Tier-3 ISPs advertise all peer routes to their upstream providers
Customer-provider links dictate how routes are exported and preferred
Peering agreements at Tier-1 eliminate the need for BGP
questions.explanation:
Customer-provider and peering relationships determine which routes an AS prefers and which neighbors receive its advertisements. Customer routes are commonly preferred and exported broadly; peer/provider routes are usually restricted to customers. Consequently, route propagation follows business relationships as well as topology. A tier label does not exempt any network from BGP or reserve filtering exclusively for one ISP tier.

See [Business relationships and export policy](../lessons/01_routing/18_bgp_export_policy.md).

questions.question: Why do ISPs carefully distinguish between transit and peering relationships in BGP?
options: To control revenue and limit unpaid traffic exchange
To enforce TCP congestion control at the interdomain level
To isolate OSPF and RIP policies within their domains
To decide which routes are loopback-eligible
To increase TTL across AS boundaries
questions.explanation:
Transit is normally a paid service providing reachability beyond a customer's network, while peering exchanges agreed traffic between networks and their customer cones. Distinguishing these relationships allows an ISP to prefer revenue-generating routes and avoid offering unpaid third-party transit. The distinction is enforced through route-selection and export policies rather than TCP congestion-control settings or packet TTL adjustments.

See [Business relationships and export policy](../lessons/01_routing/18_bgp_export_policy.md).

questions.question: How do design goals differ between edge routers and core routers?
options: Core routers dynamically learn MAC addresses; edge routers statically route packets
Edge routers implement NAT; core routers encrypt control traffic
Edge routers support diverse interfaces; core routers optimize high-speed forwarding
Edge routers minimize latency by avoiding packet queuing
Core routers emphasize access control lists; edge routers focus on throughput

questions.question: Why is diagnosing control-plane failures in interdomain routing inherently difficult?
options: Routing policies are decentralized and often opaque across ASes
Route oscillation is enforced by ICMP type 11
BGP hides route advertisements from RIBs
Routing loops only manifest under symmetric NATs
FIB lookups require synchronized clock sources
questions.explanation:
No single operator controls or sees all inter-domain routing decisions. Each AS applies its own policy and reveals only selected reachability and path information, so an observed failure can arise from remote choices that are not directly inspectable. This combination of decentralization and policy opacity makes diagnosis difficult even when every local protocol implementation is behaving as configured.

See [Why BGP uses paths and policy](../lessons/01_routing/15_bgp_path_vector.md).

questions.question: Why is ICMP critical for Path MTU Discovery (PMTUD), and what happens when it is filtered?
options: Filtering ICMP causes BGP to advertise stale prefixes
ICMP delivers DNSSEC keys used for secure tunnel setup
PMTUD switches to MPLS labels when ICMP is dropped
PMTUD fails, leading to blackholing of packets larger than the actual MTU
Filtering ICMP enables TCP Fast Open to detect firewalls
questions.explanation:
In classic IPv4 PMTUD, a packet too large for a downstream link with DF set must be discarded, and ICMP feedback tells the sender that its size is unsuitable. If this feedback is filtered, the sender may keep transmitting oversized packets that disappear while smaller traffic succeeds. That is a PMTUD black hole; it does not mean every alternative method of discovering a usable packet size also requires ICMP.

See [Fragmentation and path MTU](../lessons/01_routing/03_fragmentation_and_pmtu.md); [ICMP, ping, and traceroute](../lessons/01_routing/05_icmp_and_diagnostics.md).

questions.question: Why do modern routers apply rate-limiting to ICMP messages?
options: To conserve TTL values across Ethernet domains
To avoid checksum collisions during fast packet switching
To prevent routers from being overwhelmed by reflection-based attacks
To limit diagnostic tool effectiveness for security purposes
To prioritize DNS over ICMP in routing decisions

questions.question: What is a key tradeoff in using tunneling and overlay routing?
options: It improves BGP convergence by exposing underlying physical topology
It increases link-layer collision domains while simplifying prefix aggregation
It enables policy-based redirection but adds encapsulation overhead and path opacity
It reduces latency by flattening AS hierarchies
It allows direct multicast replication but prevents route summarization
questions.explanation:
Encapsulation adds an outer header, so the packet consumes more bytes and leaves less room under a given path MTU. It also makes the intervening network appear as a virtual link to the inner protocol, hiding some underlying path detail. Steering through selected tunnel or segment endpoints can express policy, but does not automatically shorten paths or expose the full physical topology.

See [Coexistence, encapsulation, and historical 6to4](../lessons/03_ipv6/19_tunnelling.md); [Extension-header deployment and SRv6](../lessons/03_ipv6/18_extension_deployment_and_srv6.md).

questions.question: What is a challenge associated with using anycast for load balancing?
options: Anycast routes are ignored by interior routing protocols
It disables DNS resolution due to routing ambiguity
Client sessions may break if routed to different replicas due to path changes
Anycast requires TCP options to indicate state sharing
It requires all routers to synchronize TTLs to avoid loops
questions.explanation:
Anycast routes the same destination address to one of several service instances. A routing change can move later packets to a different instance, which may lack the state of an existing connection. Long-lived sessions therefore need a design that tolerates or avoids that movement. Anycast does not itself synchronize server state or guarantee that every packet in an arbitrary connection reaches one replica.

See [Anycast, DNS selection, and service continuity](../lessons/03_ipv6/15_anycast.md).

questions.question: Which routing technique allows an AS to influence how incoming traffic enters its network in a multihomed setup?
options: Filtering traceroute packets to shape AS-PATH lengths
Modifying link-layer framing to suppress inbound flows
Assigning different TTLs to provider links
Increasing path MTU values in outbound BGP messages
Using prefix-specific advertisements to upstream providers

questions.question: How does BGP typically detect an upstream link failure in a multihomed AS?
options: By comparing DSCP values in forwarded packets
By monitoring TCP RTT spikes from internal traffic
By loss of BGP keepalives, triggering session teardown and route withdrawal
By checking TTL values in DNS replies from transit providers
Via periodic ICMP probes to loopback interfaces
questions.explanation:
BGP KEEPALIVE and qualifying UPDATE messages provide evidence that a peer session is alive. With a nonzero negotiated Hold Timer, prolonged absence of that traffic causes session failure and withdrawal of its learned reachability. A direct link or TCP failure can be detected sooner, and one missed KEEPALIVE alone does not necessarily trigger teardown. These are control-session checks, not DNS TTL or DSCP monitoring.

See [BGP messages, routing state, and next hops](../lessons/01_routing/16_bgp_messages_and_state.md).

questions.question: How do the routing goals of BGP and OSPF differ?
options: OSPF aggregates prefixes across AS boundaries; BGP does not
BGP emphasizes policy and reachability; OSPF targets shortest-path performance
OSPF prefers policy-based routing, while BGP focuses on convergence speed
BGP optimizes for latency; OSPF balances economic incentives
BGP relies on LSAs, while OSPF uses path vectors
questions.explanation:
**Supplementary (†):** This answer uses teaching marked supplementary in the supplied guide.

BGP selects permitted reachability between independent ASes, where commercial and administrative policy can outweigh path length. OSPF is an intra-AS link-state protocol that computes shortest paths using the AS's link-cost model. Thus the keyed contrast is policy/reachability versus internal least-cost routing, not BGP optimizing universal latency or OSPF replacing AS-level policy.

See [Why BGP uses paths and policy](../lessons/01_routing/15_bgp_path_vector.md); [OSPF areas and protocol operation](../lessons/01_routing/14_ospf.md); [Link-state routing and shortest paths](../lessons/01_routing/10_link_state.md).

questions.question: What challenge can arise when routers obtain IP configuration dynamically in large networks?
options: Duplicate IP address assignment due to lack of DHCP coordination
ICMP echo replies are blocked by default until loopback is configured
Routing loops form before the router's DNS cache is initialized
They may use inconsistent TTLs for OSPF updates
The FIB becomes corrupted when NAT is enabled during boot

questions.question: What happens when TTL expiry ICMP messages are dropped during a persistent forwarding loop?
options: The router resets BGP sessions with downstream peers
The forwarding loop continues silently, consuming bandwidth and CPU
The packets fragment and evade TTL checks
The source host correctly re-routes the packets via a backup path
The DNS resolver reassigns a new IP to the target host
questions.explanation:
**Review note:** Losing the ICMP Time Exceeded reply hides diagnostic feedback, but the expired packet is still discarded if TTL processing is correct. The bad forwarding entries can continue looping subsequent packets, consuming resources until routing state is corrected. The preserved key is defensible only in that ongoing-traffic sense; it must not imply the same expired packet survives because its ICMP reply was dropped.

See [Routing loops and poison reverse](../lessons/01_routing/12_routing_loops.md); [Reading an IPv4 header](../lessons/01_routing/02_ipv4_header.md); [ICMP, ping, and traceroute](../lessons/01_routing/05_icmp_and_diagnostics.md).

questions.question: Why is end-to-end debugging across multiple ASes inherently difficult?
options: Because MPLS tags are encrypted by upstream routers
Because routers discard RIB entries after 64 seconds
Because NAT prevents loopback-based traceability
Because DSCP rewrites interfere with BGP MED values
Because policies and state are private, and visibility is limited at AS boundaries
questions.explanation:
An AS normally exposes selected prefix reachability and path attributes, not its full internal topology, routing state, or commercial policy. Debugging an end-to-end path across several ASes therefore requires reasoning with incomplete information from multiple independent operators. This visibility limit is intrinsic to the administrative boundaries; it is not explained by invented fixed RIB expiry times or by mandatory encryption of path labels.

See [Why BGP uses paths and policy](../lessons/01_routing/15_bgp_path_vector.md).

questions.question: How does subnetting influence a host’s decision to use ARP or routing?
options: Subnet masks disable ICMP processing for remote hosts
All destinations outside the default gateway are forwarded using DNS resolution
Hosts apply NAT logic before consulting the subnet mask
Hosts use ARP only if the TTL exceeds 128
If the destination is within the same subnet, ARP is used to resolve MAC addresses
questions.explanation:
A host compares the destination with its own prefix to decide whether the destination is on-link. On an ordinary Ethernet subnet, it resolves an on-link destination's MAC address with ARP. For a remote destination, it selects a gateway and resolves that gateway's local MAC instead. ARP still occurs locally in both cases; DNS does not supply the remote next-hop Ethernet address.

See [IPv4 addresses, prefixes, and ARP](../lessons/01_routing/04_addressing_and_arp.md).

questions.question: How can prefix filtering protect against accidental or malicious prefix advertisement in BGP?
options: It enforces packet size limits to prevent data exfiltration
It disables ECMP to avoid load imbalance during attacks
It increases TCP port randomization for BGP sessions
It enables GRE tunneling for sensitive AS_PATHs
It restricts routing updates to prefixes authorized by the local AS policy
questions.explanation:
A prefix filter restricts accepted or exported route advertisements to prefixes permitted by the operator's policy. That can stop accidental or malicious announcements outside the intended scope before they affect route selection or propagate further. It is a control-plane check, not a packet-size limit, and its protection depends on maintaining a correct policy rather than blindly trusting every neighbor's advertisement.

See [Business relationships and export policy](../lessons/01_routing/18_bgp_export_policy.md).

questions.question: What is a key benefit of Internet Exchange Points (IXPs) in global Internet architecture?
options: They allow content providers to bypass DNS caching
They enable routers to support MPLS by default
They guarantee reachability across all Tier-1 networks
They eliminate the need for BGP sessions
They reduce latency and transit costs by facilitating direct interconnection

questions.question: What is a tradeoff of using distributed route computation in interdomain routing?
options: It increases load balancing accuracy at the expense of control-plane convergence
It improves fault isolation but complicates end-to-end policy enforcement
It enables per-packet load balancing by default
It eliminates the need for loop detection
It ensures shortest-path routing independent of policy

questions.question: What risk arises from excessive growth of routing table entries in core routers?
options: Memory exhaustion leads to dropped or default-routed traffic
Routers reset TTLs at each hop
Control-plane loops form due to duplicate BGP IDs
OSPF and BGP merge into a hybrid routing protocol
RIB entries get overwritten by FIB events

questions.question: What is the main tradeoff in tuning a routing protocol for high responsiveness?
options: It increases routing updates, potentially destabilizing the network
It improves control-plane convergence but reduces memory usage
It avoids route flap damping
It eliminates BGP MED values
It enables automatic prefix summarization
questions.explanation:
A highly responsive routing process reacts quickly to observed changes, but reacting to every short fluctuation can create many updates and repeated route changes. That churn can complicate management and disturb higher-layer behavior such as TCP RTT estimation. Operators therefore balance recovery speed against stability; faster reactions do not guarantee fewer updates or eliminate policy-driven oscillation.

See [Convergence, failures, and stability](../lessons/01_routing/22_convergence.md).

questions.question: How does AS-PATH help prevent routing loops in BGP?
options: It ensures only symmetric paths are accepted
It guarantees that shortest-path trees are formed
It ensures that only stub ASes receive default routes
The AS-PATH controls TTL expiry thresholds
Routers discard updates containing their own AS number
questions.explanation:
An AS normally adds its own ASN when advertising an ordinary route externally. If a route later returns containing that ASN in AS_PATH, the receiving AS can recognize that the advertised path would revisit itself and reject it. This is AS-level route-loop detection. It does not promise a shortest-path tree or replace the separate TTL mechanism used on data packets.

See [Why BGP uses paths and policy](../lessons/01_routing/15_bgp_path_vector.md).

questions.question: Which of the following correctly explains why IP fragmentation can negatively impact overall network efficiency?
options: Each fragment travels with its own transport-layer header, increasing overhead
Fragment loss requires retransmission of the entire original packet
Fragmented packets always arrive out of order and must be reassembled by routers
IP routers automatically reassemble fragments mid-path, increasing latency
Fragmented packets bypass congestion control, leading to uncontrolled bursts
questions.explanation:
**Review note:** The destination needs every fragment to reassemble the original datagram, so losing one fragment can waste the delivery work of all the others. IP does not request or retransmit the missing fragment itself; recovery, if any, comes from a higher layer and may cause data to be sent again. The preserved key needs that qualification. Each fragment has an IP header, not necessarily a complete transport header, and intermediate routers normally do not reassemble the datagram.

See [Fragmentation and path MTU](../lessons/01_routing/03_fragmentation_and_pmtu.md).
